about: Every turtle bottles community care, geolocates along humanitarian drift corridors, and feeds open dashboards that coordinate relief without borders.
about_paragraph1: The Hope Turtle Project is a decentralized, ecological and open-source solution to getting hope across seas to humans who need it.
about_paragraph2: Guided by open-source, earthen and subaltern principles, the hopeTurtles project combines low-tech and high-tech ingenuity with high-impact humanitarian logistics. The project centers on small, autonomous marine drones—nicknamed Hope Turtles—engineered to carry aid payloads and building materials across bodies of water using readily available materials (i.e. recovered bottles), open-source hardware (i.e. raspberry pis) and inexpensive organic materials (i.e. bamboo).
about_paragraph3: Guided by these principles, a hope turtle can be inexpensively made and assembled collaboratively just about anywhere. Folks with electronics skills can assemble the opensource hardware. Meanwhile, anyone anywhere keen to make a real, physical contribution to a humanitarian crisis can contribute the food-filled aid bottles that the hopeTurtle will be assembled with. By cutting through the politics or borders and blockades, it enables humans to connect directly to other humans with a real-life gift.
about_paragraph4: Each Turtle is designed to operate independently or in coordinated flotillas, guided by GPS and onboard microcontrollers that log their journey and transmit telemetry data back to a shared, transparent database. By studying ocean currents, the right release points for hope turtles can be discerned and individuals, communities and flotillas can release them accordingly.
about_paragraph5: At its heart, the project aims to demonstrate how community-built, ecologically principled technology can bridge distances and deliver hope across seas—without fossil fuels, military infrastructure, or centralized control. By inviting local makers, engineers, and communities to replicate, adapt, and deploy their own Hope Turtles, the movement fosters decentralized collaboration and resilience. It’s not just about robotics or transport—it’s a living experiment in applying collective compassion, ecological ethics, open-source design to global challenges.
about_body_p1: The Hope Turtle Project is a regenerative, open-source humanitarian initiative that designs and deploys small solar-powered marine vessels to deliver aid across open water to people who need it most. Rather than relying on centralised logistics or political permission, the project takes a radically different approach — building a decentralised, community-powered system where anyone, anywhere in the world can take direct, meaningful action to help a fellow human being.
about_body_p2: Each Hope Turtle is a buoyant marine vessel built primarily from bamboo and repurposed bottles — materials that are widely available, inexpensive, and biodegradable. Inspired by ancestral Austronesian seafaring traditions, the design harnesses ocean currents, wind, and solar energy rather than fossil fuels. Version 1.0 is a hand-assembled structure that carries six food-filled bottles as payload. Version 2.0 integrates onboard electronics, GPS navigation, telemetry, and self-steering — enabling independent voyages across hundreds of kilometres of open sea.
about_body_p3: Supporting the physical vessels is the hopeTurtles.org human-to-human platform — a transparent, open-source web application that connects senders and recipients directly. People in need can request specific items; supporters around the world respond by packing a bottle, registering it with a unique serial number, and dispatching it. When a turtle arrives, the recipient can look up their sender and share news of its safe arrival — creating a living record of solidarity and connection.
about_body_p4: The project is grounded in Earthen ecological principles and a commitment to radical transparency and non-violence. All designs, source code, and research are publicly available. The vessels are engineered to be as organic and biodegradable as possible — so that even if a turtle ends its journey unexpectedly, it leaves behind nutrition rather than pollution. This regenerative philosophy extends to the platform, the community, and the culture of the project itself.
about_body_p5: The Hope Turtle Project is not simply a technology project — it is an invitation. An invitation to imagine and embody a world in which compassion travels freely across borders and oceans. By keeping costs low and designs open, the project is built to grow: engineers, makers, sailors, and communities everywhere are invited to build their own Hope Turtles, commission deployments, and join a growing global bale of people committed to turning concern into care. Every turtle in the water is a small, humble, powerful act of hope.

report_negative: We also genuinely appreciate any negative feedback: turtles that landed somewhere they were not meant to, caused any trouble, or were found lost or adrift at sea. Honest reports — good or bad — make the whole project safer and more effective for everyone.

turtleos_aside: And it's why we call our babies “turtles”!
turtleos_body_p1: Inspired by other great autonomous marine vehicle projects around the world, we've developed the navigation system for the Hope Turtles from scratch to be fundamentally different from “drone” technology. Traditional drone technology is all about achieving great precision and control — with little thought for the ecosystems, animals, and humans in the environments where they are manufactured, navigated, and discarded. This is precisely why you won't find the word “drone” anywhere else on this site.
turtleos_body_p2: TurtleOS is the brains embedded in each one. Coded in MicroPython, we explored a whole range of microprocessors and settled on developing specifically for the Xiao ESP32-S3. However, we build on a hardware abstraction layer — which means you can still operate and develop TurtleOS on a Raspberry Pi or an Arduino.
turtleos_body_p3: TurtleOS provides not only the navigation algorithm for the deployment of a turtle in the open sea, but also the means to recover detailed sensory telemetry for testing, improvement, and tracking. That said, first and foremost TurtleOS is designed to navigate without an internet connection on the open seas. Using the simplest sensory setup — a GPS and a gyroscope — the turtle can control its sail servo to self-navigate toward a heading.
turtleos_body_p4: Unlike a drone, this simple system is not about precision. It's about arrival on coastal zones within a range of plus or minus 5 kilometers. Because of this, turtles can be random and powerful blessings when they arrive and are discovered by our fellow humans — but they can never be precise delivery systems or weapons.
turtleos_body_p5: To make things easy, plug in your Xiao ESP32-S3, open a terminal, and run our installer script. Already flashed? Pull the latest navigation system onto your turtle at any time with the sync script — both are ready to copy in the boxes alongside.

eco_banner_lead: The regenerative heart of every Hope Turtle — a wood-slat frame that binds food-filled bottles into a seaworthy shell.
eco_intro_p1: The heart of the hope turtle is its ecojoiner. Ecojoiners are developed by the Global Ecobrick Alliance as a means to connect bottles into super-practical cubic matrixes for arranging modular structures. Ecojoiners go particularly well with ecobricks — however they can work with any bottle as long as it is nice and full. In this way, bottles and ecojoiners can create cubic chairs, tables, shelves, and all sorts of furniture — and they can also serve as the substructure for earth and ecobrick walls.
eco_intro_p2: Over here, the human2human project has put ecojoiners to use for a new purpose: holding hope-bottles together. It turns out that PET bottles are also fantastic for containing dry food of all kinds in marine conditions.
eco_intro_p3: Using a single ecojoiner, a Hope Turtle can hold five to six 1.5-litre bottles packed with food. We've tested it — and because bottles seal so well, even in sun and sea, they can preserve their contents for weeks!
eco_intro_p4: Knowing the tides and currents, a simple six-bottle turtle can be deployed to float in to its destination.
eco_intro_p5: Optionally, at the top of the turtle, the sixth bottle can be what we call a control bottle: a cut 1.5L PET bottle that houses our specially designed sail mechanism, microcontroller unit, and power system.
eco_intro_p6: The Global Ecobrick Alliance first tried making ecojoiners out of recycled plastic (failure!), then bamboo (way better!), and finally settled on a design that uses wood slats. Unlike bamboo, wood can be sourced just about anywhere in the world. As long as it's the right size — slats from shipping pallets, plywood, or thin boards — it can be transformed with a band saw into a set of flat slats that assemble into our hexa-cube ecojoiner.
eco_note_body: Did you know you can find 85mm 1.5L bottles just about anywhere in the world? Yep — our team has researched it! The brand may vary, but without fail, 1.5L water bottles tend toward a diameter of 85mm. So far we've been able to find matching bottles in pretty much every country we've needed to. This is important: consequently, we've designed our ecojoiners to be compatible with 1.5L bottles with short bottle necks.

gen_hero_blurb: Use our system to generate custom 2D carpentry specs and 3D CNC and printer files for your bottle.
gen_notice_title: Woohoo! Our ecojoiner generator is now operational.
gen_notice_body: We're still working out the bugs, so bear with us if exports aren't quite ideal yet. 🙏
gen_p1_desc: Choose the perfect local bottle for your ecojoiner
gen_p1_body: Choosing the correct bottle type for your turtle (and future constructions with turtles and bottles!) is key. Not all bottles are ideal. The best tend to be tall and thin, rather than short and stubby. Crucial is that the bottles have short top and bottom tappers and have bodies with flat, upright sides. You can use any bottle size, but for the moment we are recommending 1.5L bottles that are between 83mm and 87mm in diameter. Our research shows that type of generic water bottle size is pretty consistent around the world.
gen_p1_alt: Choosing the right bottle for an ecojoiner
gen_p2_desc: Specify the key dimensions of your bottle
gen_p2_body: Bottles come in all shapes and sizes. Ecojoiners must adapt! Please measure carefully the key dimensions of your bottle and set them here. All dimensions are in millimetres (mm).
gen_p3_desc: Ecojoiners can be built from just about anything flat
gen_p3_body: Ecojoiners are best built with organic material that is between 8mm and 25mm thick. The best for ocean durability is solid wood boards. Do not use plastic as it will degrade into polluting the ocean and shore. Avoid metal as it will decrease buoyancy.
gen_p3_alt: Choosing a material for the ecojoiner
gen_p4_desc: Choose how you'll be fabricating your ecojoiners
gen_p4_body: Ecojoiners can be made in all sorts of ways. With your selected specs we will generate the file type you need to move ahead with carpentry, 3D printing, laser cutting or CNCing.
gen_fab_cnc_desc: For CNC machines and laser cutters (DXF)

gen_p5_desc: Pick which ecojoiner you want to build
gen_p5_body: There are more and more types of ecojoiners to choose from.
gen_fb_volume_big: This bottle size might be too big for our generator's logic.
gen_fb_volume_small: This may be too small for the system.
gen_fb_tapper_long: That's a long top tapper — not an ideal bottle type. Aim for under 15%.
gen_fb_tapper_tall: A touch tall — ideally the top tapper is under 15% of the height.
gen_fb_bottom_deep: That's a deep bottom tapper — not the ideal bottle type.
gen_fb_material_solid: Nice. This will last months at sea.
gen_fb_material_pallet: Great choice! Pallette wood is easy to find around the world, organic and often free! Look for boards under 1.5cm thick.
gen_fb_material_proto: Good for prototyping. Duration at sea is weeks.
gen_fb_material_plastic: Not a good choice. Plastic will degrade into microplastics and toxins in the ocean environment. Remember our goal is that turtles are 95% organic. Please jump straight to carpentry even for prototyping.
gen_fb_thickness_bad: That thickness doesn't look right — aim for 8–25mm.
